title: Farmers in the forest
teaches: Leafcutter ants and their fungus gardens

blocks.text: In the 1860s an English mining engineer named Thomas Belt spent four years running gold mines in the forests of Chontales, in central Nicaragua. In his spare hours he watched the animals, and the ones that interested him most were the leafcutter ants. Long columns of them marched along cleared paths to a tree, cut out pieces of leaf with their jaws, and carried them home held over their heads like sails. A colony could strip a young tree overnight. Belt's gardeners at the mine fought them constantly.

Everyone assumed the ants ate the leaves. Belt dug into their nests and saw that they didn't. The leaf pieces were cut small, chewed into a pulp, and packed into spongy masses in underground chambers, and the masses were threaded with the fine white strands of a fungus. In his book *The Naturalist in Nicaragua*, in 1874[^belt], Belt suggested that the ants were using the leaves as manure for the fungus, and eating the fungus.

blocks.caption: A leafcutter ant carrying a piece of leaf home.

blocks.text: Belt was right. In 1893 the German botanist Alfred Möller, working in southern Brazil, grew the fungus from leafcutter nests and found that it formed small swollen tips on its strands, which the ants harvest and feed to their larvae. The fungus does not grow anywhere outside the nests. The ants plant it, feed it, weed it and carry it to new colonies, and in return it is their only food.

The farm runs at a huge scale. A mature colony of the largest leafcutters, the genus *Atta*, can hold several million workers in a nest with hundreds of underground chambers, and the ants dig out tonnes of soil to make it. Different jobs fall to workers of different sizes, from soldiers with large heads and jaws, to the medium-sized cutters and carriers, to the smallest workers, which tend the fungus in the chambers. Some of these tiny workers ride home on the leaf pieces, guarding the carriers against parasitic flies that try to lay eggs on them[^flies]. In the forests of Central and South America, leafcutter ants are among the biggest plant-eaters of all, though it is their fungus that actually digests the leaves.

When a young queen leaves to start a colony, she carries a pellet of the fungus in a pouch inside her mouth. After mating she digs a chamber, spits out the pellet, and tends it, feeding it at first with her own droppings, until her first workers can go out and cut leaves. Every garden is a cutting from her mother's, which was a cutting from her grandmother's, back through millions of years.

Ants of this group, the fungus-growing ants, live only in the Americas. Comparing their DNA, biologists have traced their family tree back to a single ancestor that began growing fungus around 50 to 60 million years ago, when the forests were recovering from the asteroid that ended the age of dinosaurs. The earliest farmers grew their fungus on dead leaves, insect droppings and other litter, as many small fungus-growing ants still do. Cutting fresh leaves came much later, perhaps within the last 20 million years.

People invented farming about 12,000 years ago. Termites in Africa and Asia also farm fungus in their mounds, and some beetles that bore into wood farm fungus in their tunnels[^others]. Each of these is a mutualism like lesson 9's acacia and its ants, in which each partner pays and each gains. The fungus has lost the ability to live on its own, much as maize can no longer spread its seeds without people.

Any farm with a single crop, grown densely, attracts pests. In 1999 the Canadian biologist Cameron Currie, then a graduate student working in Panama, found that the ants' gardens were attacked by another fungus, called *Escovopsis*, found nowhere except in the gardens of fungus-growing ants. It feeds on the crop fungus, and an infected garden can be overrun and destroyed.

Currie also looked closely at a whitish crust that coats parts of many workers' bodies. It turned out to be a colony of bacteria, of a group famous among people for making antibiotics, and the bacteria made a chemical that killed *Escovopsis* while sparing the crop. The ants feed the bacteria from glands under the crust. So the leafcutter farm involves at least four players: three partners, the ants, their crop and the bacteria that act as a living weedkiller, and one enemy, the weed. The ants also weed by hand, picking out infected pieces of garden and dumping them in waste chambers[^waste].

blocks.caption: A fungus garden over four months: the ants' crop grows on the leaves brought in, the weed fungus grows by feeding on the crop, and the ants and their bacteria kill the weed. A model.
blocks.task: Remove the bacteria and watch the garden

blocks.text: The model shows why the bacteria matter. With them, weed spores keep landing but never take hold. Without them, the ants' hand weeding is too slow: the weed grows on the crop it is eating, faster as it spreads, until the garden collapses. With no garden, the colony starves.

blocks.caption: Five questions on fungus farms
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: What do leafcutter ants do with the leaves they cut?
choices: Chew them into pulp to feed a fungus, which they eat
Store them to eat through the dry season
Line their nests to keep them warm
items.why: Belt guessed it in 1874 by digging into the nests. The leaves are manure for the crop.

items.ask: How does a new leafcutter colony get its fungus?
choices: The young queen carries a pellet of it from her mother's nest
Workers find it growing on fallen logs
Workers steal it from another colony
items.why: She keeps the pellet in a pouch in her mouth and plants it in her first chamber.

choices: A fungus that attacks the ants' crop
A fungus that grows on the ants' bodies
items.why: It is a weed found only in the gardens of fungus-growing ants.

items.ask: In the figure, why does the garden collapse without the bacteria?
choices: The ants can't weed fast enough, and the weed grows by eating the crop
The bacteria were the ants' food
items.why: Hand weeding alone kills too little. The more crop the weed eats, the faster it grows.

items.ask: Roughly how long have ants been farming fungus?
items.why: DNA traces the fungus-growing ants to an ancestor of that age. People began farming about 12,000 years ago.

summary: **Leafcutter ants don't eat leaves.** Belt guessed in 1874 that they feed them to a fungus, which they eat.
**The fungus lives only in their nests.** Each young queen carries a pellet of it from her mother's garden.
**Ants have farmed fungus for 50 to 60 million years.** People began farming about 12,000 years ago.
**A colony is a factory of millions.** Workers of different sizes cut, carry, guard and garden.
**The crop has a weed.** The fungus Escovopsis lives only in ant gardens and can destroy them.
**Bacteria on the ants kill the weed.** Ants, crop and bacteria work together against the weed.

flies.title: The hitchhikers
flies.text: Phorid flies hover over leafcutter columns and dart down to lay an egg in a carrier ant; the larva eats the ant from inside. A small worker riding on the leaf fends them off with its legs and jaws, which is why so many leaf pieces have a passenger.

others.title: Other farmers
others.text: Fungus-growing termites in Africa build mounds that hold combs of chewed plant matter on which their fungus grows; the mounds' tall chimneys help ventilate the nest. Ambrosia beetles carry fungus spores in special pockets and plant them in the tunnels they bore in wood.

waste.title: Waste chambers
waste.text: Leafcutters keep their rubbish, spent garden and dead ants in separate chambers or heaps outside, tended by older workers that are kept away from the garden. The division keeps disease away from the crop and from the young.

belt.title: Belt and Darwin
belt.text: Darwin read The Naturalist in Nicaragua and called it the best of all the natural history journals ever published. Belt also described the acacias guarded by ants, the subject of lesson 9, and the little food bodies the trees grow for their ants are called Beltian bodies after him.
